title: Tell it slant
hookLine: tell all the truth but tell it slant; truth must dazzle gradually
tomorrow: who is nobody, and why would Dickinson want to be one?

cards: Some families have a blunt one, the uncle who says exactly what he thinks and calls it honesty. Dickinson wrote a short poem that seems to argue the other way. Tell all the truth, she says, but tell it slant.
Slant? From a poet this exact? Isn't telling it slant just lying with good manners?

teach.b: Read the whole poem and the puzzle solves itself. Notice the word all. She isn't saying hide part of it.
She's talking about how to deliver all of it.
Success, she says, lies in circuit: going round, not straight at. Why? Because the truth's superb surprise is too bright for our weak delight.
The way lightning is eased for children with a kind explanation, the truth has to dazzle gradually, or everyone would go blind. That's the teaching: the whole truth, at a pace a person can take in.
Not less truth; a gentler road to it. And Dickinson wrote this way herself. Her poems circle their subjects.
Death arrives as a gentleman with a carriage. Hope is a bird. She rarely says the thing straight out, and the indirection is exactly what makes it land.
Spin bends the truth to protect the teller.
Slant bends the road to protect the hearer, and still arrives at all of it.

how: Some readers of Dickinson quote this poem when they talk about delivering hard news with care; teachers use it to show how her poems approach a subject sideways.

o: telling the whole truth by a gentle, gradual road
a sloped writing desk Dickinson used at her window
a polite habit of hiding bad news from friends

games.q: the truth, by a gentle road: tap the pairs.

s: 'tell it slant' means it's fine to leave out the hard parts
she says tell all the truth; only the road bends.
Dickinson compares the truth to lightning explained kindly to children

games.q: your friend's band asks for honest feedback on a song that isn't working. what fits Dickinson?
o: say all of it, starting where they can hear it: what works, then what doesn't.
say it's great; slant means sparing feelings by skipping the problem.
list every flaw at once; honesty means no softening at all.
games.why: slant is not skipping. all of the truth arrives; the road just curves so it can be heard.

practice: Choose one truth you owe someone and haven't said. Plan the circuit, not the escape: where you'll start, what they'll need to hear first, and the gentle words that lead to all of it. Then say the first sentence quietly to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Tell it slant: Dickinson's way of telling all the truth by a gentle circuit, so it dazzles gradually instead of blinding.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: tell it slant. All of it, at a pace a heart can take. See you soon.

sources.ref: Tell all the truth but tell it slant (Johnson 1129; Franklin 1263)
